chain.g: easily managed, held, or handled; apt; skillful

ety.text: Old French ablebor. Middle English able English able From Middle English able, from Old Northern French able, variant of Old French abile, habile, from Latin habilis (“easily managed, held, or handled; apt; skillful”). Doublet of habile.
From Middle English ablen, from Middle English able (adjective).

From the first letter of the word. Suggested in the 1916 United States Army Signal Book to distinguish the letter when communicating via telephone, and later adopted in other radio and telephone signal standards.

senses.d: Having the necessary powers or the needed resources to accomplish a task.
ex: She is able to lift the box without assistance.

senses.d: Free from constraints preventing completion of task; permitted to; not prevented from.
ex: In a democratic world you'd be able to say what you thought wherever you were.
I'll see you as soon as I'm able.

senses.d: Gifted with skill, intelligence, knowledge, or competence.
ex: The chairman was also an able sailor.
He is able to practice law in six states.

senses.d: Capable of performing all the requisite duties; as an able seaman.
Having the physical strength; robust; healthy.
ex: After the past week of forced marches, only half the men are fully able.
As the hands are the most habil parts of the body...
He was born to an able family.

senses.d: To give power to; to reinforce; to confirm.
The letter "A" in Navy Phonetic Alphabet.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish diestro, from Latin dextrum (“right”).
From Latin habilis (“suitable, skillful”). Cognate with English able.
Latin capācembor. Spanish capaz Borrowed from Latin capācem (“capable, able”). Compare Portuguese capaz, Galician capaz, French capace, English capacious.
